To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) V1Net is a novel computational model of cortical recurrent processing that can learn to perform object recognition tasks from natural images; and (2) V1Net learns biologically plausible connectivity patterns, such as association fields, that are important for visual perception.

(1) the introduction of neurally inspired horizontal connectivity patterns into deep neural networks leads to a significant increase in robustness to perceptual noise, as measured by the Texturized challenge, and (2) the introduction of these connectivity patterns leads to a significant improvement in the performance of state-of-the-art deep neural network models on the task of boundary detection, as measured by performance on the BSDS500 dataset.

(1) the Texturized challenge is a new benchmark to measure the robustness of object recognition algorithms to perceptual noise; (2) the V1Net model is the best performing algorithm on the Texturized benchmark; (3) a V1Net trained to perform boundary localization in natural scenes exhibits biologically plausible connectivity patterns.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of recurrent processing principles for visual recognition, and their potential for improving the state-of-the art in computer vision.
the development of computational models inspired by primate vision and their application to computer vision.
the study of the computational role of horizontal connectivity in the primate visual cortex and its potential for the development of more biologically plausible artificial intelligence systems.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the proposed V1Net model, with a set of neurally inspired horizontal recurrent connections, is able to learn robust representations of natural images that are invariant to the presence of perceptual noise.
the proposed V1Net model with horizontal connections outperforms the control models on the Texturized challenge.

the proposed V1Net architecture, with the inclusion of neurally inspired horizontal connectivity, can be a promising candidate to improve the performance of deep neural networks for object recognition and boundary detection.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we present V1NET -- a novel convolution-recurrent unit that incorporates neurally inspired horizontal connectivity patterns to improve object recognition performance under naturalistic perceptual distortions.

we present a novel computational model of primate cortical horizontal connections that can be incorporated into standard convolutional networks to improve performance under naturalistic perceptual noise, and that such a model exhibits biologically plausible horizontal connectivities.

we have developed an AI system that learns to perform boundary detection from natural image inputs by emulating several key features of primate visual cortical organization, and that this model outperforms a number of carefully selected state-of-the-art control models on the Texturized challenge.
The main takeaway from our work is that
recurrent processing in neural networks is an important tool in learning robust representations that are invariant to environmental inconsistencies.

the primate visual system has developed a sophisticated set of mechanisms to combat perceptual noise, and we believe that such mechanisms can be leveraged to improve the performance of state-of-the-art deep neural networks.
recurrent contextual processing principles inspired by biological visual systems can be successfully incorporated into deep convolutional architectures for robust and efficient object recognition.
